name: Shake Weight

lead: The Shake Weight is a dumbbell with spring-mounted weights that oscillate when shaken, used in roughly six-minute routines for the arms, shoulders and chest. It was marketed for toned, defined upper arms, and works by making the muscles contract against the back-and-forth motion.

Independent studies measured muscle activity with electromyography. A 2011 report in the Journal of Sports Science and Medicine and a 2012 study comparing it with traditional dumbbells examined its claims; Consumer Reports found some chest, shoulder and triceps exercises inferior to conventional ones.

paras: Users hold the device in one or both hands and shake it in short sets for biceps, triceps, shoulder and chest movements. A women's version weighs 2.5 pounds and a men's version 5 pounds. Routines were sold as a few minutes per day.

Overuse injuries are possible with any repetitive exercise. A 2015 case report describes a 53-year-old man who developed an axillary vein thrombosis after a week of daily use and needed endovascular treatment.

chain: Rapid muscle contractions in biceps, triceps and shoulders
angle.text: Users run short daily routines to work the arms and shoulders, aiming for a more toned look. As a light resistance tool, it adds upper-body muscle activity for beginners without gym equipment [1].

lead: The Shake Weight is a modified dumbbell in which spring-loaded weights oscillate as the user shakes it, intended to increase muscle contractions during short upper-body workouts for toned arms, shoulders and chest [1][2]. It debuted in July 2009 through infomercials, first as a product designed for women at 2.5 pounds, with a 5-pound men's version following [1][2].

Grokipedia credits South African entrepreneur Johann Verheem and his company Fitness IQ with the invention and reports a launch price of $19.95 and over two million units sold by August 2010 [1]. The product became widely parodied, including on Saturday Night Live and The Daily Show [2].
Researchers have measured its muscle activity with electromyography and compared it to ordinary dumbbells in the Journal of Sports Science and Medicine [3][4].

paras: The device is a plastic bar with spring-mounted weights at each end. Shaking it makes the weights oscillate, and the user's muscles contract to control the motion. The standard routine includes one-handed biceps and shoulder shakes and two-handed triceps and chest shakes, typically in a session of about six minutes [1].

The Shake Weight debuted in July 2009 and clips of its infomercial went viral online; the men's version arrived in 2010 [1][2]. In September 2010 actress Emma Stone commented on it during Jimmy Kimmel Live, and the product was parodied across television and film [2].

A 2012 study in the Journal of Sports Science and Medicine compared electromyographic muscle activity during Shake Weight exercises with traditional dumbbell exercises, testing the product's claim of building strength in less time [4]. An earlier 2011 paper in the same journal asked whether the device lives up to its advertising [3]. Grokipedia summarises a related American Council on Exercise study as finding higher overall muscle activity than with equivalent dumbbell exercises, and the journal work as showing greater total upper-body activation than light dumbbells without clear superiority in targeted muscles [1].

Wikipedia reports that a 2011 Consumer Reports evaluation found exercises with the device inferior to conventional exercises for the chest, shoulders and triceps, similar for biceps, and lower in calorie burn than walking at 3 mph [2].

A 2015 case report describes a 53-year-old man who developed painful swelling of the right arm after a week of daily exercise with an oscillating dumbbell. Imaging showed an occlusive thrombus in the axillary, brachial and basilic veins, treated with thrombolysis, thrombectomy, angioplasty and stenting [5].

timeline.event: Shake Weight debuts through US infomercials [1][2].
Men's version introduced; viral parody coverage grows [1][2].
Studies and a Consumer Reports evaluation examine its claims [2][3].
Case report of axillary vein thrombosis linked to use [5].
